source.post_text:
Total solar eclipses provide a unique opportunity to study the Sun, and on Aug. 12, we'll take to the skies to learn more.

NASA-funded teams will study the eclipse with a high-flying research jet and scientific balloons: https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/heliophysics/nasa-science-soars-during-august-total-solar-eclipse/?utm_source=TWITTER&utm_medium=NASA&utm_campaign=NASASocial&linkId=991121966

replies.text: Research jets and balloons are such elegant compromises: above much of the atmosphere, below orbital cost, and mobile enough to chase totality. Which measurement benefits most from the extra observing time—the corona, ionosphere, or something less obvious?
replies.author: @SmithStation1

replies.text: Those high-flying platforms sound ideal for catching the corona details that vanish so quickly from the ground. Curious how the balloon data will complement the jet runs on atmospheric effects.

decoy_rationale: The reply feels slightly too polished and explanatory in neatly linking the platforms to specific science goals, with an oddly balanced structure.
